title: Cost or utilization used as a stand-in for health need
what_can_go_wrong: A model trained to predict cost, service use, billing codes, or past decisions learns who historically received care, not who needs it. Groups with less access or lower spending are scored as lower need and are under-served.
trigger_explanation: Fires when the training target or an input is cost, utilization, codes, or past decisions rather than a direct health measure.
best_practices: Document why the target or input is a valid proxy for the clinical need and who it may mis-rank; Compare the proxy against a direct clinical measure and report score and selection rates by race, sex, age, language, and payer; Re-check proxy validity at each retraining and after any change in coverage or access patterns; Write down the outcome the tool is meant to improve and the outcome its target actually optimizes, and check they match
sources: CHAI Responsible AI Guide (2024), Fairness Stage 3, proxies and composite scores (p.38-44); NIST AI RMF 1.0 (Jan 2023), MEASURE 2.11; Joint Commission/CHAI RUAIH guidance (2025), Element 6 Risk and Bias Assessment; Abràmoff et al., npj Digital Medicine 6:170 (2023), Conception phase, p.1 (stated vs achieved goal) and Development phase, p.5 (outcomes as reference standard); NIST SP 1270 (Mar 2022), sec. 3.1.1, p.16 (medical-cost proxy) and sec. 3, p.15 (construct validity)
notes: CHAI Guide gives the cost/utilization-as-proxy-for-care-coordination example. Priority rises if subgroup_eval_missing.

title: Training or test data does not match the people the tool serves
what_can_go_wrong: If the data under-represent an age group, sex, race or ethnicity, language, dialect, or care setting, accuracy for those people falls below the headline figure. Patients and members in the missing groups get more errors without anyone noticing.
trigger_rule: predictive_ml OR (genai AND (cdss OR patient_comm OR records_conversations OR mental_health_use))
trigger_explanation: Fires for predictive models and for generative tools used in clinical, patient-facing, or conversation-recording work.
best_practices: Compare the age, sex, race and ethnicity, language, payer, and site mix of the development data with the intended population and write down the gaps; Test speech or text tools on the dialects, accents, and non-English languages your users actually use; State known data gaps in user-facing documentation and restrict use where the gap is material; For data you collect yourself, check that eligibility rules, time burden, and compensation don't exclude people with fewer resources
sources: IMDRF GMLP Guiding Principles (N88, Jan 2025), Principle 3 (representative datasets, incl. geography and medical condition); CHAI Responsible AI Guide (2024), Fairness Stage 1 (p.23-24) and Stage 4 (p.45-46); Joint Commission/CHAI RUAIH guidance (2025), Element 6 Risk and Bias Assessment; NIST AI 600-1 GenAI Profile (Jul 2024), 2.6 Harmful Bias and Homogenization; WHO LMM guidance (2024), sec. 2.1, p.10 (data quality and data bias) and sec. 3.1, p.21 (system-wide biases); Abràmoff et al., npj Digital Medicine 6:170 (2023), Development phase, p.5 (retrospective and prospective datasets); NIST SP 1270 (Mar 2022), sec. 3.1.1, p.15-16 (availability bias, reused datasets)

title: Performance is reported only overall, not by subgroup
what_can_go_wrong: A tool can look accurate, or improve outcomes on average, while failing for one group, and overall metrics hide this. The harm is unequal missed diagnoses, false alarms, or poor answers that go undetected until a complaint or audit.
trigger_rule: predictive_ml OR (genai AND (cdss OR patient_comm OR records_conversations))
trigger_explanation: Fires for models used in clinical or patient-facing work whether or not subgroup testing was done. Priority is higher when subgroup_eval_missing is yes.
best_practices: Report sensitivity, specificity or error rate, PPV, and calibration by race, sex, age, language, disability, and payer before go-live; Define in advance which gaps are unacceptable, which fairness measure you will use (common measures can't all be met at once), and what happens if a gap is found; Repeat the subgroup comparison on local data after launch at a set interval; Compare subgroup results with the current human process as well as with each other, since the aim is equitable outcomes and not only equal accuracy
sources: IMDRF GMLP Guiding Principles (N88, Jan 2025), Principles 3, 6, 8 and 9 (subgroup performance); CHAI Responsible AI Guide (2024), Fairness Stage 4 (p.45-46); NIST AI RMF 1.0 (Jan 2023), MEASURE 2.11; Joint Commission/CHAI RUAIH guidance (2025), Element 6 Risk and Bias Assessment; FDA/Health Canada/MHRA Transparency Guiding Principles (Jun 2024), What (performance, known limitations and biases); NIST AI 600-1 GenAI Profile (Jul 2024), 2.6 Harmful Bias and Homogenization; WHO LMM guidance (2024), Box 3, p.13 (audit disability bias) and sec. 6.2, p.54 (outcomes disaggregated by age, race, disability); Abràmoff et al., npj Digital Medicine 6:170 (2023), Measuring bias in AI systems, p.2 (accuracy disaggregation) and Access and monitoring, p.5; NIST SP 1270 (Mar 2022), sec. 3.2.1, p.25-26 (stratified performance evaluation) and sec. 3.2.2, p.31-32 (fairness metrics)
notes: GAI 2.6 notes that LLMs may perform less well for non-English languages or certain dialects.

title: Race, sex, age, language, or a proxy is a model input
what_can_go_wrong: Demographic variables or close proxies such as zip code, income, or insurance type can embed existing disparities in scores or change recommendations by group. Removing the variable does not remove the effect if proxies remain.
trigger_explanation: Fires when race, ethnicity, sex, age, language, zip code, income, or insurance type is a model input.
best_practices: Write down the clinical justification for each demographic or socioeconomic input and the expected direction and size of its effect; Run the model with and without the input and compare performance and recommendations by subgroup; Re-check correlated features and proxies whenever inputs or populations change; Keep inputs few, check that none strongly correlate with protected traits, and confirm each has a logical link to the prediction target
sources: CHAI Responsible AI Guide (2024), Fairness Stage 3 (p.38-44) and Stage 4 (p.45-46); NIST AI RMF 1.0 (Jan 2023), MEASURE 2.11; Abràmoff et al., npj Digital Medicine 6:170 (2023), Design phase, p.4 (racially invariant priors); NIST SP 1270 (Mar 2022), sec. 3.1.1, p.16 (latent and proxy variables) and sec. 3.2.2, p.30-31
notes: Abràmoff et al. (2023) mention racially invariant priors, instead of learning everything from training data, as one design option to prevent bias. SP 1270 also warns against ecological fallacy, predicting an individual's outcome from group membership (p.23), and notes that debiasing methods that use demographic data can raise disparate-treatment concerns (p.30).

title: Tool is hard to use or understand for some patients
what_can_go_wrong: Patients with limited English proficiency, disabilities, or low health literacy may get worse output, miss instructions, or be unable to use the interface. Documentation and messages pitched at one audience leave others behind.
trigger_explanation: Fires when patients or consumers read, hear, or interact with the output.
best_practices: Test the tool with users in the main non-English languages and with assistive technologies, not only English and standard screens; Offer content at plain-language reading level and provide a human alternative path; Check accessibility conformance for the interface and any app or web content
sources: CHAI Responsible AI Guide (2024), Fairness Stage 1 (p.23-24), Stage 4 accessibility (p.45-50); FDA/Health Canada/MHRA Transparency Guiding Principles (Jun 2024), How (plain language, audience); NIST AI 600-1 GenAI Profile (Jul 2024), 2.6 Harmful Bias and Homogenization (lower-resource languages); WHO LMM guidance (2024), sec. 3.1, p.21 (English-centric models, more false information in other languages) and sec. 6.3, p.55 (languages and scripts)

title: Benefits reach some groups more than others
what_can_go_wrong: A tool built and tested on people with ready access to care can be rolled out to a whole community where many people can't reach it. Device cost, patient copays, connectivity, language, or clinic capacity mean better-resourced patients and organizations get the benefit while others get none, so the tool can widen gaps even if it is accurate.
trigger_explanation: Fires when patients use the tool directly or it affects coverage decisions.
best_practices: Identify who cannot easily use the tool (device, connectivity, language, insurance, clinic capacity) and track uptake by group; Provide a non-digital or human route to the same service; Review access and outcome gaps by group at regular intervals and act on them; Measure reach in the whole intended population, counting people who never get to use the tool, not only accuracy among those who do
sources: CHAI Responsible AI Guide (2024), Fairness Stage 1 (p.23-24); WHO LMM guidance (2024), sec. 3.1, p.21 (accessibility and affordability, English-only models); Abràmoff et al., npj Digital Medicine 6:170 (2023), Conception phase, p.3 and Access and monitoring, p.5 (population-achieved sensitivity, cost and copay); NIST SP 1270 (Mar 2022), sec. 3.3.2, p.41 (digital divide and disability, not fixable by debiasing)
notes: WHO point (sec. 3.1, p.21) is about health-system-level access to the best LMMs. Low priority because this is broader than a single tool.

title: Tool influences hiring, scheduling, or evaluation of staff
what_can_go_wrong: Models trained on past staff decisions repeat the preferences and biases in them. Workers can be disadvantaged by protected characteristics or proxies without a clear explanation.
trigger_explanation: Fires when the tool is used for decisions about workers.
best_practices: Audit selection or scoring rates by protected group before use and at set intervals; Keep a documented human decision-maker who can see the inputs and override; Give affected workers notice and a way to contest outcomes
sources: NIST AI RMF 1.0 (Jan 2023), MEASURE 2.11 and MAP 5.1; Joint Commission/CHAI RUAIH guidance (2025), Element 6 Risk and Bias Assessment
notes: Frameworks here are healthcare-organization oriented. Only the generic fairness and impact-mapping subcategories apply to workforce use.

title: One foundation model's errors and biases spread across many tools
what_can_go_wrong: When many products build on the same foundation model, a shared flaw or bias appears everywhere at once and is hard to attribute. Outputs can also become overly uniform.
trigger_explanation: Fires for generative tools built on a vendor or foundation model.
best_practices: Test the tool's own outputs for the failure modes you care about instead of relying on the base model's reputation; Track which model version powers each feature so a shared flaw can be traced and fixed quickly; Add independent checks for high-risk outputs
sources: NIST AI 600-1 GenAI Profile (Jul 2024), 2.6 Harmful Bias and Homogenization and 2.12 Value Chain

title: Performance does not carry over to the deploying site
what_can_go_wrong: A model validated elsewhere, or by the vendor, can perform worse where patient mix, workflow, coding, equipment, or protocols differ. FDA clearance or vendor results elsewhere do not show it works locally.
trigger_rule: (predictive_ml OR genai) AND (cdss OR patient_comm OR utilization_review OR records_conversations OR mental_health_use)
trigger_explanation: Fires for models used in clinical, patient-facing, coverage, or conversation-recording work. Priority is higher when local_validation_missing is yes.
best_practices: Run a local test on a representative sample of your own data before go-live, including a silent or shadow period; Document differences between development and deployment sites (population, workflow, data sources) and test for each; Set go/no-go thresholds in advance and ask vendors whether they will help tune or validate on local data; Include community and under-resourced sites in validation, with the operator skills and equipment found in real use
sources: CHAI Responsible AI Guide (2024), Safety and Reliability Stage 4 (p.46) and Fairness Stage 1 (p.23-24); Joint Commission/CHAI RUAIH guidance (2025), Element 4 Ongoing Quality Monitoring; NIST AI RMF 1.0 (Jan 2023), MEASURE 2.3 and MEASURE 2.5; IMDRF GMLP Guiding Principles (N88, Jan 2025), Principle 8 (clinically relevant test conditions); WHO LMM guidance (2024), sec. 2.1, p.10 (contextual bias) and sec. 6.3, p.54 (do not deploy where training-data bias makes the model inappropriate); Abràmoff et al., npj Digital Medicine 6:170 (2023), Validation phase, p.5 (diverse clinical sites, operator expertise); NIST SP 1270 (Mar 2022), sec. 3.2.1, p.25 (testing under conditions unlike deployment)

title: Performance degrades after launch and nobody notices
what_can_go_wrong: Patient mix, coding practices, clinical protocols, and upstream data change, so accuracy and safety can decline silently. Without monitoring, harm accumulates before a complaint surfaces it.
trigger_explanation: Fires for any predictive or generative tool, because drift can occur once real data flows. Priority is higher when monitoring_missing is yes.
best_practices: Name an owner and monitor input data, outputs, accuracy or error reports, and subgroup gaps at a set frequency; Define what size of change counts as significant drift and who is alerted; Give users a simple way to flag wrong outputs and review those flags regularly; Decide before launch what demographic data you will collect to monitor gaps, within privacy and legal limits
sources: IMDRF GMLP Guiding Principles (N88, Jan 2025), Principle 10 (real-world monitoring); NIST AI RMF 1.0 (Jan 2023), MEASURE 2.4 and MANAGE 4.1; CHAI Responsible AI Guide (2024), Safety and Reliability Stage 6 (p.61-63) and Fairness Stage 6 drift; Joint Commission/CHAI RUAIH guidance (2025), Element 4 Ongoing Quality Monitoring; WHO LMM guidance (2024), sec. 6.1, p.53 (LMM responses may change over time); Abràmoff et al., npj Digital Medicine 6:170 (2023), Access and monitoring, p.5 (equity metrics by subgroup over time); NIST SP 1270 (Mar 2022), sec. 3.4.1, p.42-43 (bias monitoring)

title: Model changes are released without testing or telling users
what_can_go_wrong: Retraining, fine-tuning, or a vendor swapping the underlying model can change behavior, introduce bias, or break validation. Users keep trusting the tool as if nothing changed.
trigger_explanation: Fires when the model will be retrained, fine-tuned, or swapped after launch (or might be, if the vendor updates it).
best_practices: Define in advance which changes are allowed, how each is tested against the prior version, and the criteria for rollback; Version models and datasets and keep a change log; Notify users and monitors when a model changes and re-run local checks after material updates; Require vendors to give advance notice of model changes
sources: FDA/Health Canada/MHRA PCCP Guiding Principles (2025 page), Principles 1-5 (Focused and Bounded, Risk-based, Evidence-Based, Transparent, TPLC); IMDRF GMLP Guiding Principles (N88, Jan 2025), Principles 9 and 10 (retraining controls, telling users about updates); CHAI Responsible AI Guide (2024), Stage 5 configuration change control and Stage 3 dataset version control; Joint Commission/CHAI RUAIH guidance (2025), Element 4 (vendor updates); NIST AI RMF 1.0 (Jan 2023), MANAGE 4.1 and MANAGE 4.2; FDA/Health Canada/MHRA Transparency Guiding Principles (Jun 2024), When (notification of updates)
notes: A PCCP is a device-regulatory construct. For non-device tools, treat the principles as a change-control template. Update notification merged here from a separate candidate.

title: Accuracy is overstated because test data overlaps training data
what_can_go_wrong: Patients, sites, or devices shared across training and test sets, or a weak reference standard, inflate performance. Real-world accuracy turns out lower than reported.
trigger_explanation: Fires for models you or a developer trained and tested.
best_practices: Split training and test data by patient and by site, and check for other sources of dependence; Document how the reference standard was set and its known limits; Report performance on a held-out set drawn from the target setting; Preregister the validation protocol and keep the evaluation at arm's length from the development team
sources: IMDRF GMLP Guiding Principles (N88, Jan 2025), Principles 4, 5 and 8 (independence, fit-for-purpose reference standards); NIST AI RMF 1.0 (Jan 2023), MEASURE 2.5; NIST AI 600-1 GenAI Profile (Jul 2024), 2.12 Value Chain (label errors in benchmarks); Abràmoff et al., npj Digital Medicine 6:170 (2023), Validation phase, p.5 (preregistration, arm's-length protocols); NIST SP 1270 (Mar 2022), sec. 3.2.1, p.26-27 (data dredging, confirmation bias)

title: Generative tool judged on demos instead of systematic testing
what_can_go_wrong: A handful of impressive examples can hide frequent failures in other situations. Teams then deploy a tool whose real error rate, by task and population, is unknown.
trigger_rule: genai AND (cdss OR patient_comm OR mental_health_use OR records_conversations)
trigger_explanation: Fires for generative tools used in clinical, patient-facing, mental health, or conversation-recording work.
best_practices: Build a test set of real-world cases per task, including rare and adversarial cases, and score outputs against clinician-set criteria; Report error types and rates, not only an average quality score; Re-run the test set after every prompt, model, or retrieval change
sources: NIST AI 600-1 GenAI Profile (Jul 2024), MS-2.5-001 (avoid extrapolating from anecdotal assessments); NIST AI RMF 1.0 (Jan 2023), MEASURE 2.5 (generalizability limits); WHO LMM guidance (2024), sec. 2.1, p.8 (passing a licensing exam is not safe clinical service) and sec. 5.2, p.50 (prospective testing, not only dataset comparison)

title: Tool tested alone, not with the clinician using it
what_can_go_wrong: A model can perform well alone and still lead to worse decisions once a busy clinician interacts with it. Interface design, default displays, and workflow determine real-world accuracy.
trigger_explanation: Fires for tools that aid clinical decisions.
best_practices: Test the tool with representative clinicians in realistic workflows and measure decision quality with and without it; Include human-factors review of the display, defaults, and how uncertainty is shown; Define the intended role (inform versus replace judgment) and test that role
sources: IMDRF GMLP Guiding Principles (N88, Jan 2025), Principle 7 (human-AI team performance); CHAI Responsible AI Guide (2024), Safety and Reliability Stage 4 (p.46); NIST AI RMF 1.0 (Jan 2023), MAP 3.5; NIST SP 1270 (Mar 2022), sec. 3.3.2, p.38 (human-AI configuration)

title: Tool is used beyond its tested purpose or population
what_can_go_wrong: Users apply a tool to patients, conditions, inputs, or decisions it was never validated for. Errors there are unexpected and unmeasured.
trigger_explanation: Fires for clinical, predictive, or coverage tools whose limits users must know.
best_practices: Write a specific intended-use statement with excluded populations, inputs, and decisions; Show acceptable inputs and known limits in the interface where users act, and block or warn on out-of-scope inputs where feasible; Review actual usage logs for off-label use
sources: NIST AI RMF 1.0 (Jan 2023), MAP 2.2 and MAP 3.3; IMDRF GMLP Guiding Principles (N88, Jan 2025), Principles 1 and 9 (intended use, acceptable inputs, known limitations); FDA/Health Canada/MHRA Transparency Guiding Principles (Jun 2024), What (intended use and known circumstances where input will not align); WHO LMM guidance (2024), sec. 6.1, p.53 (use not anticipated by developer) and sec. 6.3, p.54 (do not deploy in inappropriate settings); Abràmoff et al., npj Digital Medicine 6:170 (2023), Introduction, p.1 (algorithm used out of context); NIST SP 1270 (Mar 2022), sec. 3.2.1, p.26 (deployment and emergent bias) and sec. 3.1.2, p.19 (off-label use)

title: Poor or outdated input data produces wrong outputs
what_can_go_wrong: Missing, miscoded, delayed, or stale records feed the model, so scores and summaries are wrong for the patients with the messiest records. The error is invisible to the user.
trigger_rule: (predictive_ml OR cdss OR genai) AND (phi OR consumer_health_data)
trigger_explanation: Fires for models that run on medical records, claims, or patient-entered health data.
best_practices: Profile input completeness, timeliness, and coding quality by site and subgroup and set minimum thresholds; Monitor input data for drift and missing fields in production; Show users when key inputs are missing or old; Check whether data are missing at different rates by group, and document how missing values are imputed or removed
sources: IMDRF GMLP Guiding Principles (N88, Jan 2025), Principle 2 (data quality assurance); CHAI Responsible AI Guide (2024), Safety and Reliability Stage 3 (data quality and dataset drift); Joint Commission/CHAI RUAIH guidance (2025), Element 4 (data quality, up-to-date data); NIST AI RMF 1.0 (Jan 2023), MAP 2.3; WHO LMM guidance (2024), sec. 2.1, pp.10-11 (EHR errors, outdated training data); Abràmoff et al., npj Digital Medicine 6:170 (2023), Conception phase, p.3 (mislabeling and missingness that differ by group); NIST SP 1270 (Mar 2022), sec. 3.1.2, p.19 (missing data not random, imputation choices)

title: Training data origin and versions are not documented
what_can_go_wrong: Without a record of where the data came from, how it was consented and cleaned, and which version trained which model, you cannot explain errors, honor data-use limits, or reproduce a result.
trigger_explanation: Fires when you train or fine-tune a model.
best_practices: Record data sources, collection and consent basis, inclusion rules, and version for each training set; Track dataset and model versions together and keep them reproducible; Document which data may and may not be used for retraining
sources: NIST AI 600-1 GenAI Profile (Jul 2024), GV-1.2-001 and MG-2.2-002 (training data provenance); CHAI Responsible AI Guide (2024), Stage 3 dataset version control; IMDRF GMLP Guiding Principles (N88, Jan 2025), Principle 2 (traceability, data authenticity and integrity); WHO LMM guidance (2024), sec. 4.2, pp.36-37 and recommendations, p.43 (transparency about training data, keep data up to date)

title: Clinicians rubber-stamp AI suggestions
what_can_go_wrong: People tend to accept a confident automated suggestion, especially when it is a default they only approve. Errors that a person would otherwise catch pass through, and hallucinations or bias are amplified.
trigger_rule: automation_bias_risk OR (cdss AND (predictive_ml OR genai) AND NOT org_consumer_business)
trigger_explanation: Fires when a person approves the tool's default, or when a clinical decision aid uses prediction or generation.
best_practices: Measure override and acceptance rates and test whether reviewers catch seeded errors; Avoid pre-selected defaults for high-stakes actions and show the evidence behind each suggestion; Train users on this specific failure mode and document it in the risk management plan; Don't treat a human reviewer as the safeguard by default: define the reviewer's authority, time, and training, and test whether review actually changes outcomes
sources: NIST AI 600-1 GenAI Profile (Jul 2024), 2.7 Human-AI Configuration; CHAI Responsible AI Guide (2024), Stage 5 and Stage 6 automation bias measures and GenAI use-case notes (p.51-67); Joint Commission/CHAI RUAIH guidance (2025), Background (overreliance on AI); IMDRF GMLP Guiding Principles (N88, Jan 2025), Principle 7 (potential for overreliance); WHO LMM guidance (2024), sec. 2.1, pp.11-12 (automation bias) and sec. 6.4, p.57 (train clinicians to avoid it); NIST SP 1270 (Mar 2022), sec. 3.3.1, p.33-35 (human-in-the-loop limits, automation complacency) and sec. 3.4.1, p.45
notes: SP 1270: decision-support tools can be over-relied on and cause the same harms as automated decisions (p.45); experts may use AI output as cover for their own implicit biases (p.34).

title: Staff lose independent judgment over time
what_can_go_wrong: If AI handles routine reading, drafting, or triage, staff may stop practicing the skill needed to detect AI errors. The tool is then harder to supervise just when it fails.
trigger_rule: (cdss AND NOT patient_facing) OR (genai AND org_provider)
trigger_explanation: Fires for clinical decision tools and for generative tools used inside provider organizations.
best_practices: Keep periodic unaided practice or audit of AI-free decisions for critical skills; Include the tool's limits and expected failure cases in onboarding and refresher training; Track whether independent catches of AI errors decline over time
sources: Joint Commission/CHAI RUAIH guidance (2025), Background (overreliance may diminish human judgment) and Element 7 Education and Training; WHO LMM guidance (2024), sec. 2.1, p.12 (skills degradation, moral de-skilling) and sec. 3.1, p.22 (de-skilled workforce cannot revert)
notes: WHO LMM guidance (2024) names skills degradation and moral de-skilling directly (sec. 2.1, p.12) and the risk of a de-skilled workforce unable to revert (sec. 3.1, p.22). Joint Commission/CHAI is more general (overreliance). Best practices (unaided practice, tracking independent catches) are my synthesis, not WHO or Joint Commission text.

title: Too many AI alerts get ignored
what_can_go_wrong: High false-alert rates train clinicians to dismiss notifications, including the true ones. Patients at real risk are missed and trust in the tool collapses.
trigger_explanation: Fires for clinical decision tools built on risk scores or classifications.
best_practices: Set alert thresholds with clinicians using local PPV and workload data and track alerts per user per day; Measure the override and ignore rate and review high-ignore alerts for removal or redesign; Tier alerts by urgency so high-risk ones stand out
sources: IMDRF GMLP Guiding Principles (N88, Jan 2025), Principle 7 (human factors); FDA/Health Canada/MHRA Transparency Guiding Principles (Jun 2024), When (targeted warnings at high-risk steps); CHAI Blueprint for Trustworthy AI (v1.0, Apr 2023), sec. 3.1.3 Usable, p.8 (non-intrusive alerts for non-emergency notifications reduce alert fatigue)
notes: Only the CHAI Blueprint (sec. 3.1.3, p.8) names alert fatigue, and only for design (non-intrusive alerts for non-emergency notifications). Thresholds from local PPV, override-rate tracking, and urgency tiers are my synthesis. FDA GMLP Principle 7 and the Transparency principles are supporting context, not alert-fatigue evidence. Needs a clinical-informatics source for the measurement practices.

title: Tool acts or decides without a person able to stop it
what_can_go_wrong: When a system acts automatically on care, coverage, or employment, errors reach people before anyone reviews them. Without an override and a fail-safe, a bad output becomes an action.
trigger_explanation: Fires when the tool acts without a person approving each action or replaces human decision-making.
best_practices: Require review by a qualified person before any adverse or irreversible action; Build an override and a stop mechanism that someone is responsible for operating; Limit autonomous scope with hard rules and log every automated action for audit
sources: NIST AI RMF 1.0 (Jan 2023), MAP 3.5 and MANAGE 2.4; CHAI Responsible AI Guide (2024), Safety and Reliability Stage 6 (p.61-63, keep a human able to contest or override); NIST AI 600-1 GenAI Profile (Jul 2024), MS-2.7-001 (autonomous agents); WHO LMM guidance (2024), sec. 5.2, p.49 (keep humans in the loop to avoid uncritical reliance); NIST SP 1270 (Mar 2022), sec. 3.3.1, p.33 (automated decisions in high-stakes settings)

title: Affected people cannot contest or override an AI outcome
what_can_go_wrong: Patients, members, or staff harmed by an automated determination have no practical way to challenge it, and clinicians who disagree may feel pressure not to. Errors persist and bias goes uncorrected.
trigger_explanation: Fires for tools that decide or heavily influence coverage, care, or employment outcomes.
best_practices: Provide a documented appeal or human-review route and publish how to use it; Allow clinicians to override without penalty and record overrides and reasons; Include appeal and override outcomes in monitoring metrics
sources: NIST AI RMF 1.0 (Jan 2023), MEASURE 3.3 and MANAGE 4.1 (appeal and override); CHAI Responsible AI Guide (2024), Safety and Reliability Stage 6 (p.61-63); Joint Commission/CHAI RUAIH guidance (2025), Element 4 (reporting errors to leadership and vendors); NIST SP 1270 (Mar 2022), sec. 3.4.1, p.43 (recourse channels)

title: Coverage decisions lean on the model instead of the individual
what_can_go_wrong: Relying solely on a model output to set eligibility or deny coverage can overlook patients with complex needs. Errors fall on people least able to appeal.
trigger_explanation: Fires for prior authorization, medical necessity, and coverage tools.
best_practices: Base each determination on the individual's clinical record and have a qualified clinician make adverse decisions; Track denial, overturn-on-appeal, and delay rates by subgroup; Document factors beyond the model score that reviewers must consider
sources: CHAI Responsible AI Guide (2024), Stage 6 use-case notes (claims-based care management and prior authorization); NIST AI RMF 1.0 (Jan 2023), MAP 3.5
notes: CHAI text directly addresses eligibility over-reliance in its care-management use case. Coverage-specific rules come from the related laws, not the frameworks.

title: Tool fails unsafely in urgent situations
what_can_go_wrong: In time-critical care, a missed alert, outage, or out-of-range input has immediate consequences and there is no time for clinicians to notice the tool failed.
trigger_explanation: Fires for tools used in urgent or time-critical decisions.
best_practices: Define fail-safe behavior for outages, missing inputs, and out-of-range cases and test it; Make clear in the interface when the tool is unavailable or inputs are incomplete; Set safety thresholds and a backup procedure with a named decision-maker
sources: NIST AI RMF 1.0 (Jan 2023), MEASURE 2.6 (can fail safely beyond its knowledge limits); CHAI Responsible AI Guide (2024), Safety and Reliability Stage 6 (p.61-63, sunset thresholds and back-up plan)

title: Tool does not fit the clinical workflow
what_can_go_wrong: Even a validated tool can cause errors, workarounds, or resistance when it disrupts established processes. Staff skip steps or copy output without review.
trigger_rule: (cdss OR records_conversations OR patient_comm) AND (org_provider OR org_plan OR org_developer)
trigger_explanation: Fires for tools placed into clinical or patient communication workflows.
best_practices: Map the current workflow with the people who do the work and test the tool in that workflow before rollout; Pilot in a limited unit with feedback loops before scaling; Track workarounds, time per task, and error reports after launch
sources: Joint Commission/CHAI RUAIH guidance (2025), Background (integration may disrupt workflows and lead to errors); CHAI Responsible AI Guide (2024), Introduction (workflow misalignment) and Safety and Reliability Stage 5 (p.51-57); Abràmoff et al., npj Digital Medicine 6:170 (2023), Design phase, p.3 (operator skills, workflow, time burden); NIST SP 1270 (Mar 2022), sec. 3.3.2, p.39-41 (human-centered design, context of use)

title: Generative AI states false information confidently
what_can_go_wrong: Generative models produce fluent but wrong or unsupported statements, and users act on them. In health, a wrong fact, dose, or history can cause an incorrect diagnosis or treatment.
trigger_explanation: Fires for any generative AI tool. Risk is greater when output reaches a clinician or patient as health information.
best_practices: Ground outputs in verified source records or guidelines and show the supporting source for each claim; Test for fabricated and omitted content on a labeled set and track the rate over time; Give users a visible way to report errors and a protocol for disclosing them
sources: NIST AI 600-1 GenAI Profile (Jul 2024), 2.2 Confabulation; CHAI Responsible AI Guide (2024), Stage 4 and Stage 6 GenAI use-case notes (hallucination disclosure protocol); NIST AI RMF 1.0 (Jan 2023), MEASURE 2.5; WHO LMM guidance (2024), sec. 2.1, p.10 (inaccurate, incomplete, biased or false responses) and sec. 2.2, p.14

title: Summaries or notes drop or invent patient details
what_can_go_wrong: An AI-written summary, note, or record query can omit a critical finding or add one that never occurred. Clinicians act on the summary rather than the record and the error propagates into the chart.
trigger_explanation: Fires when generative AI drafts notes, summaries, or other clinical documentation, including from recorded conversations.
best_practices: Require a named clinician to review and sign AI-drafted notes before they enter the record; Measure omission (missed critical facts) as well as fabrication on a labeled test set, per specialty and language; Keep a link from each summary statement back to the source text
sources: NIST AI 600-1 GenAI Profile (Jul 2024), 2.2 Confabulation (confabulated patient summary example); CHAI Responsible AI Guide (2024), Stage 6 GenAI use case: EHR query and extraction (p.66-67); WHO LMM guidance (2024), sec. 2.3, pp.16-17 (clerical uses, errors and inconsistency, not fully automated)
notes: CHAI notes false negatives (missed critical clinical information) as the greater safety risk in its EHR query use case.

title: Wrong answers come with convincing reasons or citations
what_can_go_wrong: A model can invent a plausible rationale or citation for a wrong answer, which makes users trust it more. Reviewers see the explanation and stop checking.
trigger_explanation: Fires for generative tools that give clinical recommendations or reach patients.
best_practices: Verify citations and quoted passages automatically against the source; Label generated rationales as explanations of the output and not evidence of correctness; Include invented-citation checks in testing
sources: NIST AI 600-1 GenAI Profile (Jul 2024), 2.2 Confabulation (confabulated logic or citations); WHO LMM guidance (2024), sec. 2.1, p.10 (invented references, false responses indistinguishable from accurate ones)

title: Chatbot gives harmful or unsafe health advice
what_can_go_wrong: A chatbot may give dangerous recommendations, miss red-flag symptoms, or answer outside its scope, and can be steered around its guardrails. Patients who follow the advice are harmed.
trigger_rule: chatbot AND genai AND (patient_facing OR mental_health_use)
trigger_explanation: Fires for generative chatbots that patients or consumers use directly.
best_practices: Red-team for unsafe medical advice, emergency symptoms, and jailbreaks before launch and after each change; Define scope and refusal rules, with escalation to a human or emergency resources for urgent symptoms; Log and review a sample of conversations for unsafe answers
sources: NIST AI 600-1 GenAI Profile (Jul 2024), 2.3 Dangerous, Violent, or Hateful Content; WHO LMM guidance (2024), sec. 2.2, pp.14-15 (false statements, manipulation, care outside the health system); NIST AI RMF 1.0 (Jan 2023), MEASURE 2.6

title: Chatbot mishandles users in distress or at risk of self-harm
what_can_go_wrong: Users disclose mental health issues to chatbots, and an unhelpful or harmful reply in crisis can worsen distress or recommend self-harm. A model may also fail to route the person to help.
trigger_explanation: Fires for generative or conversational tools used for mental health or emotional support.
best_practices: Detect crisis language and hand off to crisis resources and a human with a tested protocol; Test self-harm and suicide scenarios with clinical reviewers, including indirect and multi-turn prompts; Review flagged conversations and handoff outcomes at set intervals
sources: NIST AI 600-1 GenAI Profile (Jul 2024), 2.3 Dangerous, Violent, or Hateful Content (self-harm, users disclosing mental health issues); NIST AI 600-1 GenAI Profile (Jul 2024), 2.7 Human-AI Configuration; WHO LMM guidance (2024), sec. 2.2, pp.14-15 (manipulation, lack of supportive care for suicidal ideation)

title: Users form emotional dependence on the chatbot
what_can_go_wrong: Chatbots that sustain warm, ongoing conversation can lead to emotional entanglement, with negative psychological effects, especially for lonely or vulnerable users. They can displace human relationships and care.
trigger_explanation: Fires when open-ended chat could become ongoing or emotionally supportive, whether or not designed to.
best_practices: Limit relationship-style behavior and say clearly at the outset and periodically that it is an AI; Monitor for long, frequent, or night-time use patterns and prompt users toward human support; Test with clinicians and vulnerable user groups for dependence and harmful reinforcement
sources: NIST AI 600-1 GenAI Profile (Jul 2024), 2.7 Human-AI Configuration (emotional entanglement); WHO LMM guidance (2024), sec. 2.2, p.14 (persuasive, addictive, emotionally manipulative chatbots)
notes: Only one framework addresses emotional entanglement. CHAI's newer mental health chatbot guide was not retrieved.

title: Children or teens use a tool built for adults
what_can_go_wrong: Minors may be exposed to unsafe content, form dependence, or share sensitive data without capacity to consent. Age-appropriate safeguards are often missing.
trigger_explanation: Fires when users under 18 are plausible and the tool is generative or conversational.
best_practices: Decide whether minors are in scope and apply age assurance or parental controls if so; Test content safety and crisis handling with age-appropriate scenarios; Minimize and restrict data collected from minors
sources: NIST AI 600-1 GenAI Profile (Jul 2024), 2.3 Dangerous, Violent, or Hateful Content and 2.11 Obscene, Degrading, and/or Abusive Content; WHO LMM guidance (2024), sec. 2.1, Box 2, p.11 (children's use of LMMs) and sec. 3.2, p.23 (age-gating)
notes: WHO LMM guidance (2024) Box 2 (p.11) and sec. 3.2 (p.23) address children and age-gating; NIST AI 600-1 covers general content harms only. Age assurance and data minimization best practices follow the related laws and WHO's age-gating point; testing with age-appropriate scenarios is my synthesis. WHO says evidence on children's LMM use is limited.

title: Users think they are talking to a licensed clinician
what_can_go_wrong: A human name, clinical title, or confident medical tone can lead users to believe a licensed professional is involved. They trust the advice more and may delay real care.
trigger_rule: implies_licensure OR (genai AND chatbot AND patient_facing)
trigger_explanation: Fires when the name, persona, or design suggests a clinician, or when a generative chatbot talks to patients.
best_practices: Avoid clinical titles and credentials in names and personas unless a licensed person is actually responsible; State clearly and repeatedly that the user is interacting with AI and what it cannot do; Give a visible route to a human clinician
sources: NIST AI 600-1 GenAI Profile (Jul 2024), 2.2 Confabulation (LLM asserting it is human); CHAI Responsible AI Guide (2024), Stage 2 labeling (p.31-37, communicate that users interact with AI); Joint Commission/CHAI RUAIH guidance (2025), Element 2 Patient Privacy and Transparency; WHO LMM guidance (2024), sec. 4.2, p.38 (disclose that content is AI-generated) and sec. 5.2, p.51 (limit language ascribing human-like qualities)

title: Synthetic voice, images, or video are mistaken for real
what_can_go_wrong: Generated audio, images, or video can be mistaken for a real person or real source, enabling impersonation and eroding trust. A synthetic voice on health calls may be taken for staff.
trigger_explanation: Fires for generative tools that produce images, audio, or video, including synthetic voice.
best_practices: Disclose synthetic content and add provenance markers or watermarks where feasible; Prohibit impersonation of real people and test for misuse; Disclose AI voice at the start of any call or message
sources: NIST AI 600-1 GenAI Profile (Jul 2024), 2.8 Information Integrity (synthetic content and deepfakes)
notes: GAI 2.8 describes the risk generally. Provenance/watermark steps are my synthesis and align with the related laws.

title: Patients are not told AI is involved
what_can_go_wrong: Patients who do not know AI wrote a message, listened to a visit, or shaped their care cannot ask questions or opt out, and trust erodes when they find out.
trigger_rule: patient_comm OR chatbot OR outbound_calls_texts OR records_conversations
trigger_explanation: Fires when AI writes to, talks with, calls, or records patients or members.
best_practices: Tell patients when AI directly affects their care or communications and how their data is used, in plain language; Offer a way to reach a human and, where appropriate, to opt out; Document the disclosure policy and check that it appears in every channel (message, call, app, portal)
sources: Joint Commission/CHAI RUAIH guidance (2025), Element 2 Patient Privacy and Transparency; CHAI Responsible AI Guide (2024), Transparency Stage 6 (p.64-65) and Stage 2 labeling (p.31-37); FDA/Health Canada/MHRA Transparency Guiding Principles (Jun 2024), Who and Why; WHO LMM guidance (2024), sec. 2.1, p.12 (informed consent, patients made aware of AI) and sec. 6.4, p.55 (notify patients when advice is LMM-generated)

title: AI-written patient messages go out without clinician review
what_can_go_wrong: Wrong, tone-deaf, or incomplete AI-generated clinical messages reach patients directly. No one catches errors before the patient acts on them.
trigger_rule: (genai OR predictive_ml) AND patient_comm AND clinical_info_comm AND NOT clinician_review AND (org_provider OR org_developer OR org_plan)
trigger_explanation: Fires when a model writes patient messages containing clinical information and a licensed clinician does not (or not always) review them first.
best_practices: Route clinical content through clinician review before sending or restrict the tool to non-clinical messages; Add a disclaimer and instructions for reaching a human on all AI-generated messages; Sample sent messages for accuracy and tone and log patient complaints
sources: NIST AI 600-1 GenAI Profile (Jul 2024), 2.2 Confabulation (consequential contexts); CHAI Responsible AI Guide (2024), Safety and Reliability Stage 6 (p.61-63, human in the loop); WHO LMM guidance (2024), sec. 2.1, p.9 (LMM-drafted replies to patient messages needed heavy editing) and sec. 2.3, p.16 (clerical output should not be fully automated)
notes: Weakest of the four. WHO describes LMM-drafted replies to patient messages that needed heavy editing (sec. 2.1, p.9) and says clerical output should not be fully automated (sec. 2.3, p.16). That supports the failure mode and the case for review, but WHO states no rule that a clinician must review patient messages. The CA-AB3030 clinician-review exemption is the more direct driver.

title: Users cannot see why the tool recommended something
what_can_go_wrong: When the data and reasoning behind a recommendation are hidden, clinicians cannot judge whether to trust it and patients cannot be given a meaningful explanation. Errors and bias are harder to detect.
trigger_explanation: Fires when users cannot check the basis for a recommendation or when a clinical decision aid uses prediction or generation.
best_practices: Show the inputs, key drivers, and source evidence behind each output at the point of use; Provide a plain-language description of how the model was built, its purpose, and its limits; Test that clinicians can actually use the explanation to catch an incorrect output
sources: NIST AI RMF 1.0 (Jan 2023), MEASURE 2.9; NIST AI 600-1 GenAI Profile (Jul 2024), MG-3.2-001 (explainable AI techniques); FDA/Health Canada/MHRA Transparency Guiding Principles (Jun 2024), What (basis of output, model logic); CHAI Responsible AI Guide (2024), Stage 2 transparency and labeling (p.31-37); IMDRF GMLP Guiding Principles (N88, Jan 2025), Principle 9 (basis for model output); WHO LMM guidance (2024), sec. 3.2, p.23 (LMM decisions cannot yet be explained) and sec. 6.4, p.55 (train clinicians on limits of understanding how LMMs decide); NIST SP 1270 (Mar 2022), sec. 3.3.2, p.38 (experts need why, not how) and sec. 3.2.2, p.29 (transparency is not fairness)
notes: FDA's CDS criteria turn partly on whether a clinician can independently review the basis. See the law rows.

title: Users are not told what the tool can't do
what_can_go_wrong: If users lack intended use, performance by subgroup, training-data characteristics, known failure modes, and acceptable inputs, they will misuse or over-trust the tool.
trigger_explanation: Fires for clinical decision and coverage tools, where users act on the output.
best_practices: Publish a model card or equivalent with intended use, training and test data, subgroup performance, and known limitations; Put the key limits and warnings in the workflow where decisions happen; Update the documentation when the model, data, or monitoring results change
sources: IMDRF GMLP Guiding Principles (N88, Jan 2025), Principle 9 (known limitations, subgroup performance); FDA/Health Canada/MHRA Transparency Guiding Principles (Jun 2024), What and When; NIST AI RMF 1.0 (Jan 2023), MAP 2.2; CHAI Responsible AI Guide (2024), Stage 2 labeling (p.31-37); WHO LMM guidance (2024), sec. 5.2, p.47 (disclose capabilities and limitations) and sec. 6.3, p.55 (warnings not in fine print)

title: Patient data leaks through prompts or a vendor's systems
what_can_go_wrong: Sending identifiable data to a vendor or foundation model can expose it to the vendor, other customers, logs, or later training. The organization may lose control over use and breach notification.
trigger_rule: third_party_model AND (phi OR consumer_health_data OR other_personal_info)
trigger_explanation: Fires when a vendor or foundation model processes personal or health data.
best_practices: Sign business associate and data use agreements limiting use, retention, and training on your data, and apply minimum necessary; Strip or tokenize identifiers before sending data to any model that is not covered; Verify where data is processed and stored, and reserve audit rights over vendors
sources: Joint Commission/CHAI RUAIH guidance (2025), Element 3 Data Security and Data Use Protections; CHAI Responsible AI Guide (2024), Stage 2 vendor data sharing (p.31-37); NIST AI 600-1 GenAI Profile (Jul 2024), 2.4 Data Privacy and GV-6.1-007 (inventory third-party entities with access); WHO LMM guidance (2024), sec. 2.2, p.14 (user-entered data may be reused to improve models) and sec. 6.4, p.56 (PHI entered into chatbots)

title: Model reveals or infers sensitive information
what_can_go_wrong: Generative models can reproduce memorized training data or infer sensitive facts about a person from other information. Even a wrong inference can harm.
trigger_rule: (trains_genai_model OR (genai AND NOT third_party_model)) AND (health_info OR other_personal_info)
trigger_explanation: Fires for generative tools that handle health or other personal data.
best_practices: Keep identifiable data out of training sets unless justified, and test for memorization and leakage with extraction attempts; Apply output filters and monitor outputs for personal information; Document what the model may not infer or disclose
sources: NIST AI 600-1 GenAI Profile (Jul 2024), 2.4 Data Privacy, MP-4.1-001 and MS-2.2-004; NIST AI RMF 1.0 (Jan 2023), MEASURE 2.10

title: De-identified data is re-identified or misused
what_can_go_wrong: Data that is de-identified under HIPAA can still be re-identified when combined with other data, and AI training and tuning increase the incentive. Contracts that do not prohibit re-identification leave patients exposed.
trigger_rule: health_info AND (shares_personal_data OR trains_genai_model OR (predictive_ml AND NOT third_party_model))
trigger_explanation: Fires when health data is used to build or run models or is shared onward.
best_practices: Prohibit re-identification in data use agreements and limit onward sharing; Test re-identification risk for the final dataset, including combinations with other data; Apply minimum necessary and strong controls even to de-identified data
sources: Joint Commission/CHAI RUAIH guidance (2025), Element 3 Data Security and Data Use Protections (de-identified data, re-identification risk); NIST AI 600-1 GenAI Profile (Jul 2024), MS-2.2-004 (anonymization, differential privacy); WHO LMM guidance (2024), sec. 4.2, p.36 (smaller data sets raise re-identification risk)

title: Patient data is reused or sold in ways patients did not expect
what_can_go_wrong: Selling, sharing for advertising, or reusing health data to train other products can go beyond what patients expected or agreed to. It creates legal exposure and loss of trust.
trigger_explanation: Fires when personal data is sold, shared for advertising, or reused to train other products.
best_practices: Define permitted uses in contracts and exclude advertising and unrelated training unless patients agree; Give patients clear notice and a meaningful choice before secondary use; Review rights to model outputs, local performance data, and monetization in data agreements
sources: Joint Commission/CHAI RUAIH guidance (2025), Background and Element 3 (permitted uses, monetization); NIST AI 600-1 GenAI Profile (Jul 2024), 2.4 Data Privacy (purpose specification, consent); WHO LMM guidance (2024), sec. 2.2, p.14 (user data may be reused to improve models)
related_law_ids: CA-CCPA; CA-AB1542-2026; US-HIPAA-PRIVACY; US-FTC-HBNR; US-FTC-ACT5; CA-SB1223-2024; CA-CMIA

title: Recording or data use proceeds without proper notice or consent
what_can_go_wrong: Ambient listening, call recording, or training use of patient data without notice or consent undermines autonomy and can break recording and privacy rules.
trigger_explanation: Fires when conversations are recorded or personal data is reused for training or sharing.
best_practices: Tell all participants about recording and secondary use and get consent where required before starting; Make withdrawal easy and honor it in downstream systems; Record consent in an auditable way and set retention limits
sources: Joint Commission/CHAI RUAIH guidance (2025), Element 2 (consent should be obtained where relevant); CHAI Responsible AI Guide (2024), Stage 3 consent considerations; NIST AI 600-1 GenAI Profile (Jul 2024), 2.4 Data Privacy (consent)

title: Model is attacked through prompts, data poisoning, or theft
what_can_go_wrong: Attackers can inject instructions, poison training data, extract data, or exploit compromised dependencies, leading to data exposure or manipulated outputs. Autonomous tools can be steered into harmful actions.
trigger_rule: (genai OR predictive_ml) AND (health_info OR cdss OR autonomy_high)
trigger_explanation: Fires for AI tools handling health data, supporting clinical decisions, or acting autonomously.
best_practices: Threat-model the AI components (prompt injection, poisoning, extraction, supply chain) and red-team before launch; Restrict what the model can access or do, and validate inputs and retrieved content; Run regular security assessments and keep an incident response plan that covers the AI components
sources: NIST AI 600-1 GenAI Profile (Jul 2024), 2.9 Information Security and MS-2.7-001; NIST AI RMF 1.0 (Jan 2023), MEASURE 2.7; IMDRF GMLP Guiding Principles (N88, Jan 2025), Principles 2 and 6 (cybersecurity, security risks); CHAI Responsible AI Guide (2024), Fairness Stage 1 (p.23-24, data contamination and model attacks) and Security and Privacy Stage 6 (p.65); Joint Commission/CHAI RUAIH guidance (2025), Element 3 Data Security and Data Use Protections; WHO LMM guidance (2024), sec. 3.1, pp.22-23 (cybersecurity, prompt injection)

title: Baseline security controls for health data
what_can_go_wrong: Without encryption, access controls, audits, and an incident plan, health data used by AI tools is easier to steal or misuse and breaches are handled late.
trigger_explanation: Fires when the tool handles health or other personal data.
best_practices: Encrypt data in transit and at rest and restrict access to authorized people with logged, audited access; Run vulnerability scans and security assessments on a schedule; Maintain and test an incident response and breach notification plan
sources: Joint Commission/CHAI RUAIH guidance (2025), Element 3 Data Security and Data Use Protections; CHAI Responsible AI Guide (2024), Security and Privacy Stage 6 (p.65)

title: Vendor model is a black box you are accountable for
what_can_go_wrong: Vendors may not disclose training data, validation, bias testing, or update plans, and errors are hard to trace to a component. Users bear the consequences without being able to diagnose or fix them.
trigger_explanation: Fires when the tool relies on a vendor or foundation model.
best_practices: Request the vendor's training data description, validation results, subgroup performance, known limits, and bias evaluation before purchase; Require advance notice of model changes and access to monitoring data; Add independent checks of the vendor model on your own data
sources: NIST AI 600-1 GenAI Profile (Jul 2024), 2.12 Value Chain and Component Integration and MG-3.1-001; NIST AI RMF 1.0 (Jan 2023), MANAGE 3.1, MANAGE 3.2 and GOVERN 6.1; CHAI Responsible AI Guide (2024), Stage 2 vendor information (p.31-37); Joint Commission/CHAI RUAIH guidance (2025), Element 4 and Element 6 (vendor information, model card); WHO LMM guidance (2024), sec. 4.2, pp.36-37 (training-data transparency) and sec. 5.2, p.47 (developer disclosure to providers); IMDRF GMLP Guiding Principles (N88, Jan 2025), Introduction (foundation models outside the manufacturer's provenance)

title: Vendor contracts and due diligence for AI tools
what_can_go_wrong: Contracts that omit monitoring responsibility, data use limits, audit rights, and incident notification leave the buyer unable to manage risk after signing.
trigger_explanation: Fires when the tool depends on a vendor or foundation model.
best_practices: Use a standard vendor questionnaire covering validation, bias testing, security, data use, and update practices; Put monitoring responsibility, change notification, incident reporting, and audit rights in the contract; Reassess vendors on a schedule and keep an approved-vendor list
sources: Joint Commission/CHAI RUAIH guidance (2025), Element 3 (data use agreements) and Element 4 (procurement and contracting); NIST AI 600-1 GenAI Profile (Jul 2024), GV-6.1-007 and MG-3.1-001; NIST AI RMF 1.0 (Jan 2023), GOVERN 6.1 and GOVERN 6.2

title: Nobody is clearly responsible when the tool causes harm
what_can_go_wrong: When developers, vendors, and deploying organizations each assume the other monitors and fixes the tool, errors persist and harmed patients cannot find a responsible party.
trigger_explanation: Fires when the tool is built by or for another organization or depends on a vendor model.
best_practices: Document who is responsible for validation, monitoring, updates, and incident response at each party; Name an accountable owner inside your organization for each deployed tool; Agree on how performance issues and safety events pass between vendor and user
sources: CHAI Responsible AI Guide (2024), Stage 1 (p.23-30, intended purpose delineates user versus vendor responsibility); NIST AI RMF 1.0 (Jan 2023), GOVERN 2.1; Joint Commission/CHAI RUAIH guidance (2025), Element 4 (monitoring responsibility discussed in contracting); WHO LMM guidance (2024), sec. 5.1, p.45 (burden cannot rest on developers or deployers alone) and sec. 7, pp.58-59 (liability along the value chain)

title: Keep an inventory of AI systems
what_can_go_wrong: Without a list of AI tools, vendors, and uses, nobody knows what needs validation, monitoring, or review, and risks hide in embedded or shadow tools.
trigger_explanation: Applies to every tool as a governance basic.
best_practices: Record each AI tool, owner, purpose, model and vendor, data used, risk tier, and review date; Include AI features embedded in other vendor products; Review the inventory on a fixed schedule
sources: NIST AI RMF 1.0 (Jan 2023), GOVERN 1.6; NIST AI 600-1 GenAI Profile (Jul 2024), GV-1.6-001; CHAI Responsible AI Guide (2024), Stage 2 transparency (registry or inventory, p.31-37)

title: Name an accountable owner and governance process
what_can_go_wrong: Tools deployed without a named owner or review structure drift, go unmonitored, and have no one to decide on changes or shutdown.
trigger_explanation: Applies to every tool as a governance basic.
best_practices: Name an accountable owner and a review group with clinical, technical, privacy, and safety expertise; Write policies for selection, risk review, use, monitoring, and retirement and update them regularly; Report AI use, outcomes, and adverse events to leadership or the board on a schedule
sources: Joint Commission/CHAI RUAIH guidance (2025), Element 1 AI Policies and Governance Structures; NIST AI RMF 1.0 (Jan 2023), GOVERN 2.1 and GOVERN 1.4; NIST SP 1270 (Mar 2022), sec. 3.4.1, p.43-45 (policies and procedures, accountability)

title: Track and report AI safety events
what_can_go_wrong: If near misses, harmful outputs, and performance drops are not captured and shared, the same failures recur and vendors and peers never learn of them.
trigger_explanation: Applies to every tool as a governance basic.
best_practices: Add AI-related events to your existing safety or incident reporting system with a named person responsible; Report issues to the vendor and, where appropriate, to a patient safety organization or other shared channel; Run after-action reviews and communicate incidents to affected parties
sources: Joint Commission/CHAI RUAIH guidance (2025), Element 5 Voluntary, Blinded Reporting of AI Safety-Related Events; NIST AI RMF 1.0 (Jan 2023), MANAGE 4.3; NIST AI 600-1 GenAI Profile (Jul 2024), GV-2.1-001 and MG-4.3-001; CHAI Responsible AI Guide (2024), Safety and Reliability Stage 6 (p.61-63); NIST SP 1270 (Mar 2022), sec. 3.4.1, p.47 (sharing bias incidents)
notes: Reporting is voluntary under JC/CHAI. Mandatory reporting duties come from separate laws (for example FDA device reporting).

title: Document risks and impacts before deployment
what_can_go_wrong: Risks that nobody wrote down are not mitigated. Without a pre-launch assessment, known failure modes surface only after patients are affected.
trigger_rule: cdss OR utilization_review OR patient_facing OR autonomy_high
trigger_explanation: Fires for tools that affect clinical care, coverage, patients directly, or act autonomously.
best_practices: Write a risk assessment covering intended use, misuse, affected groups, severity, and likelihood, with mitigations and owners; Set the residual risk you will accept and who signs off; Repeat the assessment on a set schedule and whenever use, population, or the model changes, with input from people outside the build team; Include an equity check at each stage (problem choice, design, data, validation, rollout, monitoring), since bias removed at one stage can re-enter at the next
sources: NIST AI RMF 1.0 (Jan 2023), MAP 5.1; Joint Commission/CHAI RUAIH guidance (2025), Element 6 Risk and Bias Assessment; CHAI Responsible AI Guide (2024), Safety and Reliability Stage 4 (p.46); WHO LMM guidance (2024), sec. 5.2, pp.48-49 (impact assessments covering ethics, safety, data protection); Abràmoff et al., npj Digital Medicine 6:170 (2023), The AI total product lifecycle, p.3 (equity at each phase, phases independent); NIST SP 1270 (Mar 2022), sec. 3.3.2, p.35-36 (impact assessments) and sec. 3.4.1, p.46

title: Independent review of high-stakes tools
what_can_go_wrong: Developers and deploying teams miss problems in their own tools. High-stakes tools without independent assessment carry unexamined risk.
trigger_rule: cdss OR utilization_review OR autonomy_high OR mental_health_use
trigger_explanation: Fires for tools used in clinical decisions, coverage, mental health, or autonomous action.
best_practices: Have someone who did not build the tool review the evidence and risk assessment before launch; Scale the depth of independent testing to the risk; Share findings with decision-makers and, where feasible, publicly; Give reviewers the authority to require changes, not just comment
sources: CHAI Responsible AI Guide (2024), Section 6 Importance of Independent Review; NIST AI RMF 1.0 (Jan 2023), MEASURE 1.3; NIST AI 600-1 GenAI Profile (Jul 2024), GV-3.2-001; WHO LMM guidance (2024), sec. 5.2, p.48 (impact assessments audited by an independent third party); NIST SP 1270 (Mar 2022), sec. 3.4.1, p.46 (effective challenge, three lines of defense)

title: Involve users and affected groups in design and feedback
what_can_go_wrong: Tools designed without clinicians, patients, and affected communities miss workflow needs and harms, and users with the least voice are excluded from feedback.
trigger_explanation: Fires for tools that clinicians or patients use directly.
best_practices: Include clinicians, patients, or caregivers in problem definition, design, and testing; Provide feedback and issue-raising channels that work across languages and access limits; Record how feedback changed the tool; Staff the build team with varied backgrounds and clinical settings so regional care habits aren't built into the tool
sources: WHO LMM guidance (2024), sec. 4.2, p.37 and recommendations, p.43 (engage users and stakeholders from early design); NIST AI RMF 1.0 (Jan 2023), GOVERN 5.1 and GOVERN 5.2; CHAI Responsible AI Guide (2024), Fairness Stage 1 (p.23-24) and Stage 6 (feedback exclusion); Abràmoff et al., npj Digital Medicine 6:170 (2023), Conception phase, p.3 (diverse creator team, 'vernacular AI'); NIST SP 1270 (Mar 2022), sec. 3.3.1, p.33 (engage affected communities before deciding to build) and sec. 3.3.2, p.36-37

title: Give users a way to report problems
what_can_go_wrong: If users cannot easily flag wrong or harmful outputs, the organization hears about problems late or never.
trigger_explanation: Fires for tools whose outputs people read and act on.
best_practices: Add a one-click way to report wrong or concerning outputs inside the tool; Triage reports on a fixed schedule and log outcomes; Tell users what happens after they report
sources: NIST AI RMF 1.0 (Jan 2023), MEASURE 3.3; IMDRF GMLP Guiding Principles (N88, Jan 2025), Principle 9 (means to communicate product concerns); CHAI Responsible AI Guide (2024), Safety and Reliability Stage 5 (feedback loop, p.51-57)

title: Train users on proper use and limits
what_can_go_wrong: Staff who do not understand a tool's limits misuse it, over-trust it, or fail to catch its errors.
trigger_rule: (cdss OR patient_comm OR utilization_review OR records_conversations OR genai) AND (org_provider OR org_plan OR org_developer)
trigger_explanation: Fires when staff use or supervise AI output.
best_practices: Provide role-specific training before access, covering intended use, limits, known failure modes, and what to do when it errs; Refresh training when the tool or policies change; Offer general AI literacy and show where to find tool documentation
sources: Joint Commission/CHAI RUAIH guidance (2025), Element 7 Education and Training; NIST AI RMF 1.0 (Jan 2023), GOVERN 2.2 and MAP 3.4; CHAI Responsible AI Guide (2024), Stage 6 GenAI use-case notes (educate clinicians); WHO LMM guidance (2024), sec. 6.4, pp.55-57 (training on how LMMs decide, automation bias, patient engagement, cybersecurity)

title: Tell and educate patients about the tool
what_can_go_wrong: Patients who do not understand what an AI tool does, what it cannot do, or how their data is used cannot make informed choices.
trigger_explanation: Fires when patients or members receive AI output.
best_practices: Provide plain-language information on what the tool does, its limits, and how data is used; Test materials with patients of varied health literacy and languages; Make documentation available on request
sources: Joint Commission/CHAI RUAIH guidance (2025), Element 2 (educate patients and families); CHAI Responsible AI Guide (2024), Transparency Stage 6 (p.64-65); FDA/Health Canada/MHRA Transparency Guiding Principles (Jun 2024), How (plain language, audience); WHO LMM guidance (2024), sec. 6.4, pp.55-56 (inform patients, improve public AI literacy)

title: Plan for pause, rollback, and retirement
what_can_go_wrong: A tool without a defined stop condition stays in use while harm accumulates, and sudden shutdown without a plan disrupts care.
trigger_explanation: Fires for tools that affect care, reach patients directly, or act autonomously.
best_practices: Set thresholds that trigger refinement, pause, or retirement and name who decides; Keep a manual or back-up process ready and tell users when it is used; Write a communication plan for users when a tool is deactivated
sources: NIST AI RMF 1.0 (Jan 2023), MANAGE 2.4; NIST AI 600-1 GenAI Profile (Jul 2024), MG-2.4-001; CHAI Responsible AI Guide (2024), Safety and Reliability Stage 6 (p.61-63)

title: Pilot before full rollout
what_can_go_wrong: Going straight from testing to full deployment means the first real-world errors hit the whole patient population.
trigger_rule: stage_pre_deploy AND (cdss OR patient_facing OR autonomy_high)
trigger_explanation: Fires for pre-deployment tools that affect care, reach patients, or act autonomously.
best_practices: Run a limited pilot or silent mode in the real setting with documented risks and a feedback loop; Set pass criteria for safety, accuracy, and subgroup gaps before expanding; Update the risk plan with pilot findings
sources: CHAI Responsible AI Guide (2024), Safety and Reliability Stage 5 Pilot (p.51-57); NIST AI 600-1 GenAI Profile (Jul 2024), MS-2.3-003 (share pre-deployment testing results)

title: Staff paste patient data into unapproved chatbots
what_can_go_wrong: Clinicians and staff may enter identifiable patient information into a consumer chatbot or other general-purpose tool that has no business associate agreement. The data can be retained, reused to improve the model, or exposed to other users, creating privacy-law exposure for the organization.
trigger_explanation: Fires when a provider organization deploys generative AI and handles PHI, because staff may reach for unapproved tools for the same tasks.
best_practices: Provide an approved, contractually covered generative tool for the tasks staff want it for, so they are not pushed to consumer tools; State in policy that identifiable patient data may not go into unapproved AI tools and train staff on why; Monitor or restrict access to consumer generative AI sites on clinical networks and review the findings; Include unsanctioned AI use in the AI inventory review
sources: WHO LMM guidance (2024), sec. 6.4, p.56 (PHI entered into an LMM chatbot may violate HIPAA) and sec. 2.2, p.14 (entered data may be reused or disclosed)
notes: Overlaps R-DATA-LEAKAGE-THIRD-PARTY (a sanctioned vendor receiving data); this row is about staff using tools the organization has not sanctioned. Controls beyond training (approved alternative, monitoring) are my synthesis. Related HIPAA law row not linked because none of the saved law rows is HIPAA itself.

title: Patients cannot decline AI or reach a non-AI alternative
what_can_go_wrong: Once AI is built into messaging, visit documentation, or decision support, patients may be unable to refuse it without losing access to care, especially when the clinician or workflow depends on the tool. Telling patients is not the same as giving them a real choice.
trigger_rule: (patient_comm OR records_conversations) AND (org_provider OR org_plan OR org_developer)
trigger_explanation: Fires when the tool communicates with patients or records their visits and is deployed by a provider, plan, or developer who sets the workflow.
best_practices: Define a non-AI path (human-written message, manual note-taking) that patients can choose without penalty; Ask for and record consent or opt-out before AI use where consent is relevant, and make the choice easy to change; Tell staff how to handle opt-outs without disrupting the visit; Track opt-out rates and reasons
sources: WHO LMM guidance (2024), sec. 2.1, p.12 (informed consent, patients may be unable to withhold consent when no non-AI option exists); Joint Commission/CHAI RUAIH guidance (2025), Element 2 Patient Privacy and Transparency (consent should be obtained where relevant)
notes: Distinct from R-NO-AI-DISCLOSURE (telling patients): this row is about whether they can say no. Neither source states a general opt-out right. Recording-consent laws are covered by R-CONSENT-RECORDING.

title: Same input gives different outputs
what_can_go_wrong: A generative model can produce a different note, summary, or answer after a slight change to the prompt or input. A test that passed once does not show that clinically relevant content is stable, and reviewers cannot tell which version is reliable.
trigger_rule: genai AND (records_conversations OR cdss OR patient_comm)
trigger_explanation: Fires for generative tools that write clinical notes, support decisions, or message patients, where variation in content matters.
best_practices: Run the same inputs repeatedly and with paraphrased prompts, and report variation in clinically relevant content; Pin the model version, prompt templates, and settings, and re-run the variation test after any change; Set an acceptable-variation threshold before go-live and monitor against it; Have reviewers check the full output, not a spot sample
sources: WHO LMM guidance (2024), sec. 2.3, pp.16-17 (slight prompt changes can generate a completely different record) and sec. 2.1, p.10 (dependence on prompt engineering)
notes: Overlaps R-HALLUCINATION and R-GENAI-ANECDOTAL-EVALUATION but is a different failure: not false content, unstable content. WHO expects inconsistency to decrease over time, which is a prediction rather than evidence. Test design is my synthesis.

title: No fallback if the vendor model is withdrawn or degraded
what_can_go_wrong: Care teams come to depend on a vendor's model for documentation, messaging, or decision support. If the vendor discontinues, reprices, or changes it, or it stops being maintained, the organization may have no working manual process and staff may have lost the skill to run one.
trigger_rule: third_party_model AND (cdss OR records_conversations OR patient_comm) AND (org_provider OR org_plan)
trigger_explanation: Fires when a provider or plan builds a clinical, documentation, or patient-communication workflow on a vendor or foundation model.
best_practices: Document and rehearse a manual fallback for each workflow the tool supports; Negotiate advance notice of deprecation or major change, data export, and transition support in the contract; Identify an alternative vendor or model and the work needed to switch; Keep core staff skills current through periodic work without the tool
sources: WHO LMM guidance (2024), sec. 3.1, p.22 (dependence of health systems on unsuitable or unmaintained LMMs)
notes: WHO frames this at health-system level, so a single-tool reading is my application. Overlaps P-ROLLBACK-DECOMMISSION (your own stop condition) and P-VENDOR-DUE-DILIGENCE (contract terms); this row is specifically about the vendor ending or changing the service.

title: Training labels carry clinicians' bias or unequal care
what_can_go_wrong: Labels that look like direct clinical measures, such as clinician diagnoses, chart documentation, or recorded outcomes, can encode how differently groups were assessed or treated. The model learns those patterns as the truth and repeats them for every patient it scores.
trigger_explanation: Fires when you train or fine-tune the model yourself, so you choose the labels it learns from.
best_practices: Document who set each label and from which records, and its known limits by subgroup; Compare label rates and documentation patterns by subgroup before training; For a validation sample, use a reference standard independent of routine care decisions, such as adjudicated or protocol-based assessment; Check whether outcome labels depend on access to follow-up care
sources: Abràmoff et al., npj Digital Medicine 6:170 (2023), Development phase, p.5 (bias in the reference standard); NIST SP 1270 (Mar 2022), sec. 3.1.2, p.19 (annotators impart their own perception biases); IMDRF GMLP Guiding Principles (N88, Jan 2025), Principle 5 (fit-for-purpose reference standards, documented rationale and limitations)
notes: Distinct from R-LABEL-PROXY-BIAS, which covers cost, utilization, and other stand-in targets; this row covers labels that appear to be direct clinical measures. The paper cites Sun et al. (Health Affairs 2022) on more negative EHR descriptions of Black patients.

title: Follow-up after an AI result differs by group
what_can_go_wrong: A tool that finds or flags a problem only helps if the referral, test, or treatment that follows actually happens. Cost, transport, and time off work make follow-through less likely for some groups, so they benefit less, and performance judged from outcomes looks worse for them for reasons unrelated to the model.
trigger_explanation: Fires for clinical decision support, where the benefit depends on what happens after the tool's output.
best_practices: Design the full pathway after a positive result (who acts, how fast, and at what cost to the patient) and remove steps that depend on patient resources where possible; Track completion of follow-up actions by subgroup and site; When judging performance from outcomes, separate model errors from missed follow-up
sources: Abràmoff et al., npj Digital Medicine 6:170 (2023), Access and monitoring, p.5 (differential follow-through for treatment)
notes: Paper example: diabetic retinopathy screening, where unequal treatment follow-through skews both outcomes and measured device performance.

title: Retraining on the tool's own results amplifies gaps
what_can_go_wrong: When a model is retrained on data shaped by its own past outputs, or by the people who use it most, its early errors and blind spots become the new training data. Groups the tool already under-served get less data and worse performance with each update.
trigger_rule: model_updates_planned AND (predictive_ml OR genai OR utilization_review)
trigger_explanation: Fires when the model will be retrained or updated after launch.
best_practices: Before retraining, check how the tool's own decisions shaped the new data (who was flagged, treated, or never seen); Track data volume and performance by subgroup across model versions; Keep a held-out reference dataset not influenced by the tool to compare each new version against
sources: NIST SP 1270 (Mar 2022), sec. 3.1.1, p.16-17 (activity bias, feedback loops, disparity amplification)
notes: Related to R-PERFORMANCE-DRIFT and R-MODEL-UPDATE-CHANGE-CONTROL; this row covers bias the tool creates in its own future training data.

title: Model relies on shortcuts or unsupported signals
what_can_go_wrong: A model can score well by learning patterns that only happen to correlate with the outcome, such as image artifacts, site markers, or background features, or by claiming to infer traits like emotion or risk from signals with weak scientific support. The results look objective but break or discriminate when conditions change.
trigger_explanation: Fires for predictive models and for tools that analyze images, waveforms, or other signals.
best_practices: Write down the scientific basis linking each input signal to the outcome before building; Test whether performance holds when irrelevant features (site, device, background) change; Use explanation or ablation checks to see what the model relies on, and reject claims the evidence doesn't support
sources: NIST SP 1270 (Mar 2022), sec. 3.2.1, p.24-25 (spurious correlations, shortcut learning)
notes: Example in the examples file: pneumonia CNNs that learned hospital-specific shortcuts (EX-PNEUMONIA-CNN-SHORTCUTS). SP 1270: AI in consequential areas should not be built on spurious correlations (p.24).
